**Q-2.1.a** Use the training dataset where the two classes are easily separable, i.e. with two separated blobs in the upper and lower left quadrant. Train your model. How well does your classifier do? Provide a screenshot of the result.

[click here](https://playground.tensorflow.org/#activation=tanh&batchSize=10&dataset=circle&regDataset=reg-plane&learningRate=0.03&regularizationRate=0&noise=0&networkShape=4,2&seed=0.62835&showTestData=false&discretize=false&percTrainData=50&x=true&y=true&xTimesY=false&xSquared=false&ySquared=false&cosX=false&sinX=false&cosY=false&sinY=false&collectStats=false&problem=classification&initZero=false&hideText=false)

Use the playground to create an architecture for logistic regression for binary classification. We'll have two inputs and one output.

![](img/Q_2.1.a_screenshot.png)

**Q-2.1.b** What are your fitted weights? Use those weights to compute (by hand) what the predicted probability for two arbitrary sample points, verify your intuition.

**Answer:**
The fitted logistic regression model is:

$$
P(y=1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b)}}
$$

Fitted weights:
$w_1 = 0.79$ | $w_2 =1.1$ | $b = 0$

**Point A: $(x_1 = 3, x_2 = 3)$**

$$
z_A = (0.89)(3) + (1.1)(3) = 5.97
$$

$$
P_A = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-5.97}} = 0.9975
$$


**Point B: $(x_1 = -3, x_2 = -3)$**

$$
z_B = (0.89)(-3) + (1.1)(-3) = -5.97
$$

$$
P_B = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-7.8}} = 0.00255
$$

**Result:**

- Point A has a low probability (~0.00255) → classified as class 0
- Point B has a high probability (~0.9975) → classified as class 1

This result is consistent with the result from the neural network space output that 2 points belong to different classes.

**Q-2.1.c** Now use the bullseye data and try to fit this data with logistic regression. Does it work? Provide a screenshot of the result.

**Answer:** With no transformations of the features and parameters setup, fitting bullseye data with logistic regression does not work well as shown in the sreenshot.
![](img/Q_2.1.c_screenshot.png)

**Q-2.1.c** Try using different transformations of the data. See if you can get logistic regression to fit this data. Can you get it to separate with a single layer?

**Answer:** Yes, by doing quadratic transformations on x1 and x2, logistic regression can already separate data very well with a single layer as shown on the screenshot below.
![](img/Q_2.1.c_screenshot2.png)


**Q-2.1.d**  Explore adding hidden layers with 2 or 3 units and fit the model with different activations. Can you get it to work perfectly? Try adding another unit to the hidden layer. Comment on what is the simplest model that can still fit this dataset. Provide a screenshot of the result

**Answer:** When adding 2 hidden layers with 3 and 2 neuron for each, and set activation as Relu, the data can be separated very well as shown in the screenshot below.
![](img/Q_2.2.d_2layers.png)

Adding the third hidden layer with 1 neuron doesn't make big impact (shown in below screenshot) as the 2 hidden layer model already perfomrs very well. The simpliest model that separate the model well is 2 hidden layers with 3 neurons on first layer and 2 neurons on the second layer. I also tried changing the activation to Tanh, which provides a sligtly better result but no meaningful difference from the Relu activation result.
![](img/Q_2.2.d_3layers.png)
